This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)

- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

# WSDL to Go

Generates Go code from a WSDL file.

## Install

* [Download release](https://github.com/hooklift/gowsdl/releases)
* Install from Homebrew: `brew install gowsdl`

## Usage

```
Usage: gowsdl [options] myservice.wsdl
  -o string
        File where the generated code will be saved (default "myservice.go")
  -p string
        Package under which code will be generated (default "myservice")
  -i    Skips TLS Verification
  -v    Shows gowsdl version
```

## Features

* Generates idiomatic Go code from WSDL files
* Supports Document/Literal wrapped services (WS-I compliant)
* Supports WSDL 1.1, XML Schema 1.0, and SOAP 1.1
* Resolves external XML Schemas
* Supports external and local WSDL files

## Note

The generated code is a reflection of what the WSDL is like. If your WSDL has duplicated type definitions, your Go code is going to have the same and may not compile.

# WSDL to Go

Generates Go code from a WSDL file.

## Install

* [Download release](https://github.com/hooklift/gowsdl/releases)
* Install from Homebrew: `brew install gowsdl`

## Usage

```
Usage: gowsdl [options] myservice.wsdl
  -o string
        File where the generated code will be saved (default "myservice.go")
  -p string
        Package under which code will be generated (default "myservice")
  -i    Skips TLS Verification
  -v    Shows gowsdl version
```

## Features

* Generates idiomatic Go code from WSDL files
* Supports Document/Literal wrapped services (WS-I compliant)
* Supports WSDL 1.1, XML Schema 1.0, and SOAP 1.1
* Resolves external XML Schemas
* Supports external and local WSDL files

## Note

The generated code is a reflection of what the WSDL is like. If your WSDL has duplicated type definitions, your Go code is going to have the same and may not compile.

	dirFlag        = flag.String("d", "./", "Directory under which package directory will be created")

	packageFlag    = flag.String("p", "myservice", "Package under which code will be generated")

	flag.Usage = func() {
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Usage: %s [options] myservice.wsdl\n", os.Args[0])
		flag.PrintDefaults()
	}
	flag.Parse()
	if *versionFlag {

	if wsdlPath == "" {

	}
	if err := run(wsdlPath); err != nil {
		fmt.Println("\U0001F340  "+err.Error())

package main

import (

func run(wsdlPath string) error {
	// Determine if URL or file via url.Parse
	u, err := url.Parse(wsdlPath)
	if err != nil {
		// To match original panic behavior? Instead return error
		return err
	}
	isURL := u.Scheme != ""
	var wsdlContent []byte
	var baseDir string
	var baseURL *url.URL
	var absDisplay string
	if isURL {
		// Log Downloading with u.String()
		fmt.Println("\U0001F340  Downloading file " + u.String())
		content, err := fetchURL(u.String())
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		wsdlContent = content
		baseURL = u
		// For server file, use original downloaded content (as is)
		// Need to handle imports recursively
		if err := fetchImportsForWSDL(wsdlContent, baseURL, nil); err != nil {
			return err
		}
	} else {
		ap, _ := filepath.Abs(wsdlPath)
		absDisplay = ap
		fmt.Println("\U0001F340  Reading file " + absDisplay)
		content, err := os.ReadFile(absDisplay)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		wsdlContent = content
		baseDir = filepath.Dir(absDisplay)
		if err := fetchImportsForWSDLFile(wsdlContent, baseDir); err != nil {
			return err
		}
	}
	// Parse WSDL
	// Need to handle all schemas including imported ones - we need to collect them
	// For now, parse main content and imported contents collected during fetch
	// The fetch functions above already logged Reading/Downloading for imports but didn't store?
	// We need to refactor to store imported schemas
	return generate(wsdlContent, baseDir, baseURL)
}

func fetchURL(urlStr string) ([]byte, error) {
	tr := &http.Transport{}
	if *insecureFlag {
		tr.TLSClientConfig = &tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true}
	}
	client := &http.Client{Transport: tr}
	resp, err := client.Get(urlStr)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	defer resp.Body.Close()
	return io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
}

func fetchImportsForWSDL(data []byte, baseURL *url.URL, visited map[string]bool) error {
	// Parse to find xsd:import/include schemaLocation and wsdl:import location
	// For simplicity, unmarshal into generic struct to find imports
	type Import struct {
		SchemaLocation string `xml:"schemaLocation,attr"`
		Location       string `xml:"location,attr"`
	}
	type Schema struct {
		Imports []Import `xml:"http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema import"`
		Includes []Import `xml:"http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema include"`
	}
	type Types struct {

	// Check qualified
	qualified := true
	if q, ok := gd.ElementFormQualified[complexNS]; ok {
		qualified = q
	} else {
		// If not found, check any? Default true (as for stock with no elementFormDefault)
		qualified = true
	}
	if !qualified {
		return ""
	}
	// Collect all refs (name, ns) for this complexType
	type ref struct{ name, ns string }
	var refs []ref
	for idx, e := range elementList {
		ns := elementNSList[idx]

func collectFieldsFromSequence(seq *Sequence, targetNS string, gd *GenData, makePublic bool) []string {
	var fields []string
	for i := range seq.Elements {
		e := &seq.Elements[i]
		fields = append(fields, genFieldFromElement(e, targetNS, gd, makePublic))
	}
	// Handle nested choices/sequences? For simplicity, flatten one level
	for i := range seq.Choices {
		ch := &seq.Choices[i]
		for j := range ch.Elements {
			e := &ch.Elements[j]
			fields = append(fields, genFieldFromElement(e, targetNS, gd, makePublic))
		}
	}
	for i := range seq.Sequences {
		s := &seq.Sequences[i]
		for j := range s.Elements {
			e := &s.Elements[j]
			fields = append(fields, genFieldFromElement(e, targetNS, gd, makePublic))
		}
	}
	// Ignore Anys
	return fields

func serverGoName(elemName string, gd *GenData) string {
    // If element has Type (alias to named type), use TYPE's Go name (public); else use element's Go name
    if e, ok := gd.ElementMap[elemName]; ok && e != nil {
        if e.Type != "" && !isBuiltinType(e.Type) {
            return publicGoName(localName(e.Type))
        }
        if e.Ref != "" && !isBuiltinType(e.Ref) {
            return publicGoName(localName(e.Ref))
        }
    }
    // Check all schemas for element (since ElementMap only has first, need to search all? For VersionInfoRequest, it's in map, good. For others, also.)
    // For inline (no type) or builtin type, use element name
    return publicGoName(elemName)
}

func serverGoType(elemName string, gd *GenData) string {
    // For server type (request/response type), similar: if element has Type custom, use TYPE; else if builtin, use element? Actually for request with builtin? Unlikely. For now same as serverGoName?
    // For VersionInfoRequest with type BaseRequest, request type is BaseRequest (same as name). Good.
    // For DivisionsRequest with inline, request type is DivisionsRequest (element). Good.
    // For CreateImage with type CreateImageType, request type is CreateImageType. Good.
    // So same as serverGoName
    return serverGoName(elemName, gd)
}
